newsitem.title: UK: UK options market buzzing after billion pound bet.
newsitem.headline: UK options market buzzing after billion pound bet.

text.p: The London options market saw fevered speculation on Wednesday over the identity of the stock market gambler who bet one billion pounds ($1.65 billion) on a market crash before the end of June next year.

The biggest-ever options trade was placed on London's International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE) on Tuesday by a mystery investor who bet a record one billion pounds on a 15 percent drop in the FTSE 100 index of leading British shares.
Market insiders said they were sceptical about press speculation that the party behind the bet was probably one of Britain's major life assurance companies.
Some dealers said it was more likely that one of the large U.S. hedge funds was behind the deal, acting through a local trader.
Most agreed the investor's identity was likely to remain one of the industry's best-kept secrets.
"No-one will ever know who is behind it unless the client reveals themselves," said one senior futures trader at a leading brokerage.
Dealers said the independent trader who carried out the transaction was a local trader who floor brokers for institutions. The trader is known to have links with life assurance clients.

"He runs a very cheap execution-only service for institutions," said the trader. "For a deal this size the commission would have been very high, so the client has looked for someone cheap to carry it out."

Sources close to the market commented that the mystery client was likely to be betting on a shake-out in the stock market around general election time, when equities are likely to be vulnerable to short-term volatility.
The next general election has to be held before the end of next May, but could be called at any time by the government.
"Basically it's a volatility trade," said one trader. "They will make money if the market moves either way...but the market has to move."
In a complex strategy the unnamed client sold June 4300 calls and bought June 3300 puts in what is called a "split synthetic" trade.
The trade at 4300 caps any possible gains whilst the 3300 puts protects or "hedges" against losses. But the position is skewed so that more money is made if the stock market crashes.

Economic strategists are divided on where the FTSE will end the year, let alone where it will be at the time of the election. Forecasts range from 3,600 to 4,200 for the end of 1996. At Wednesday's close the FTSE 100 index stood at 3,935.7. ($1=.6072 Pound)
